dev_notes: src/commands/release.mjs: cutChecks() is the one list cut, status and bare `ledger` all show, and renderChecks() draws it. The PDF is printed before releases.json is saved, so a failed print leaves nothing cut; --no-pdf skips it. A refusal is a raw UserError with exit code 3. The commit comes from HEAD, or from --commit for a retrospective cut, verified as an ancestor of HEAD. --run hands an open audit, composition or verify to an agent through runTask() in src/prompt.mjs; at a TTY the open questions are asked through askInline() before composing and again after a verify; then it asks before cutting (--yes skips that). `--skip summary,review` map to compose and verify. `release cut|list|amend` stay as aliases in src/cli.mjs.

history.name: Cutting a release
history.description: The command ledger release cut gives the release in progress its name and date and opens the next one behind it, which is where everything recorded from then on lands. The release just cut becomes an edition that never changes again, and ledger release list shows the timeline with the number of entries each release covers. Cutting a release with nothing recorded against it is refused, because the edition would be identical to the one before it.

The command ledger cut gives the open release its name and date, prints its PDF edition into the client folder, and opens the next release, where everything recorded from then on lands. Before it writes anything, it runs five checks: no redraft is waiting to be checked, no code has changed since the last audit, something is recorded, the release is reviewed, and the cut stands for a different moment from the last one. When a check is open, the cut writes nothing, lists every check with the command that fixes it, and --skip passes only the checks you name. Each cut records its commit, so two demos on one day stay two editions, and ledger releases shows the timeline with each release's commit.

The command ledger cut gives the open release its name, date and commit, prints its PDF edition into the client folder with the message to send beside it, and opens the next release. It refuses only an edition that would be wrong: one with nothing recorded, or one whose redrafted corpus hasn't been checked against the old. Anything else, such as changes the last prepare hasn't read or a reason nobody gave, it shows first and asks before it goes ahead; --yes answers when nobody is at a terminal.

events.what: A cut ran five checks. It now also waits until the release's summary is written and up to date, so an edition never opens with lists that leave out or misstate what moved, and ledger cut --run hands the summary to an agent along with the audit and the review. See “Summary of changes”.

The cut checks the composition, the opt-in verify and the open questions where it checked the summary and the review, asks open questions one at a time at a terminal, and with --run hands over an audit, a composition or a verify.
events.why: The summary and the review became one composition and an optional check against the code, and an agent's questions printed at the end of its run were gone with the terminal.

events.what: ledger cut refuses only an edition that would be wrong, with nothing recorded or a redraft not yet checked, and shows everything else as a warning before it asks to go ahead. It also writes the message to send beside the edition, and no longer hands anything to a coding agent.
events.why: The developer decides what isn't done, and the tool's job is to say it clearly. Lining up the stamps of three agent tasks, with --skip and --force to get round them, made the cut the place the workflow had to be explained, and tokens are spent only when someone asks for them.
